portal-01-queues.png.t: Queue names — your orders queue and its dead-letter queue (the one ending -dlq). ServiceHub finds every queue in the region; you do not list them.
Messages available — waiting to be received. The dead-letter queue's number is what ServiceHub counts as dead letters (here 324).
Region — queues belong to a region. You choose the same region in ServiceHub when you connect (here Asia Pacific (Mumbai), ap-south-1).

portal-02-orders-queue.png.t: URL — the address of this queue. ServiceHub builds it for you from the queue's name and your region.
Dead-letter queue — Enabled: a message that fails too often is moved to a second queue instead of being lost.
Dead-letter queue tab — shows which queue receives the failures (next screenshot).

portal-03-dead-letter-queue.png.t: Queue — the dead-letter queue that receives the failures. ServiceHub reads this one to show Dead letters.
Maximum receives — 3: after three failed tries SQS moves the message here. Reading a dead letter from ServiceHub counts as one more receive, which is why ServiceHub only looks when you ask.

portal-04-iam-users.png.t: Create user — start here to make a user just for ServiceHub, not your own.
The ServiceHub user — separate from your own, so you can switch it off later without disturbing anything else.

portal-05-user-permissions.png.t: Console access — Disabled. This user is for programs only: nobody can sign in to the AWS console as it.
Access key 1 — what ServiceHub signs in with. It is made on the Security credentials tab; AWS shows its secret only once.
servicehub-sqs — one inline policy, limited to the two queues (next screenshot). The user has no other permissions.

portal-06-policy-json.png.t: Actions — what ServiceHub may do: read queue counts, receive (to look), change visibility (to hand a looked-at message back), send and delete (to replay). Above these, sqs:ListQueues lets it find your queues.
Resource — only these two queues. If the key ever leaked, it could touch nothing else in your account.

portal-07-access-keys.png.t: Create access key — choose “Application running outside AWS”, then copy the Access key ID and the Secret access key. AWS shows the secret once.
Status — Active. Make it Inactive or delete it at any time to cut ServiceHub off.
Actions — make the key inactive or delete it: the way to revoke ServiceHub’s access later.
